{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{About|the type of transformation|the category of morphisms denoted as '''''End'''''|Endomorphism}}

In [[category theory]], an '''end''' of a [[functor]] <math>S\colon\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf{C}\to \mathbf{X}</math> is a universal [[dinatural transformation]] from an object <math>e</math> of <math>\mathbf X</math> to <math>S</math>.{{sfnp|Mac Lane|2013}}

More explicitly, this is a pair <math>(e,\omega)</math>, where <math>e</math> is an object of <math>\mathbf X</math> and <math>\omega\colon e\ddot\to S</math> is an [[extranatural transformation]] such that for every extranatural transformation <math>\beta\colon x\ddot\to S</math> there exists a unique morphism <math>h\colon x\to e</math> 
of <math>\mathbf X</math> with <math>\beta_a=\omega_a\circ h</math> 
for every object <math>a</math> of <math>\mathbf C</math>.

By abuse of language the object <math>e</math> is often called the ''end'' of the functor <math>S</math> (forgetting <math>\omega</math>) and is written

:<math>e=\int_c^{} S(c,c)\text{ or just }\int_\mathbf{C}^{} S.</math>

Ends can also be described using limits. If <math>\mathbf X</math> is [[Complete category|complete]] and <math>\mathbf C</math> is small, the end can be described as the [[Equalizer (mathematics)#In category theory|equalizer]] in the diagram

:<math>\int_c S(c, c) \to \prod_{c \in C} S(c, c) \rightrightarrows \prod_{c \to c'} S(c, c'), </math>

where the first morphism being equalized is induced by <math>S(c, c) \to S(c, c')</math> and the second is induced by <math>S(c', c') \to S(c, c')</math>.

== Coend ==
The definition of the '''coend''' of a functor <math>S\colon \mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{X}</math> is the dual of the definition of an end.

Thus, a coend of <math>S</math> consists of a pair <math>(d,\zeta)</math>, where <math>d</math> is an object of  <math>\mathbf X</math> and <math>\zeta\colon S\ddot\to d</math>
is an extranatural transformation, such that for every extranatural transformation <math>\gamma\colon S\ddot\to x</math> there exists a unique morphism
<math>g\colon d\to x</math> of <math>\mathbf X</math> with <math>\gamma_a=g\circ\zeta_a</math> for every object <math>a</math> of <math>\mathbf C</math>.

The ''coend'' <math>d</math> of the functor <math>S</math> is written

:<math>d=\int_{}^c S(c,c)\text{ or }\int_{}^\mathbf{C} S.</math>

Coends have a characterization using limits dual to the characterization of ends. If <math>\mathbf X</math> is cocomplete and <math>\mathbf C</math> is small, then the coend can be described as the coequalizer in the diagram

:<math>\int^c S(c, c) \leftarrow \coprod_{c \in C} S(c, c) \leftleftarrows \coprod_{c \to c'} S(c', c). </math>

==Examples==
===Natural transformations===

Suppose we have functors <math>F, G : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{X}</math> then

:<math>\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{X}}(F(-), G(-)) : \mathbf{C}^{op} \times \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{Set}</math>.

In this case, the category of sets is complete, so we need only form the [[Equalizer (mathematics)#In category theory|equalizer]] and in this case

:<math>\int_c \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{X}}(F(c), G(c)) = \mathrm{Nat}(F, G) </math>

the natural transformations from <math>F</math> to <math>G</math>.  Intuitively, a natural transformation from <math>F</math> to <math>G</math> is a morphism from <math>F(c)</math> to <math>G(c)</math> for every <math>c</math> in the category with compatibility conditions.  Looking at the equalizer diagram defining the end makes the equivalence clear.

===[[Simplicial_set#Geometric_realization|Geometric realizations]]===

Let <math>T</math> be a [[simplicial set]].  That is, <math>T</math> is a functor <math>\Delta^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}</math>.  The [[discrete topology]] gives a functor <math>d:\mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Top}</math>, where <math>\mathbf{Top}</math> is the category of topological spaces.  Moreover, there is a map <math>\gamma:\Delta \to \mathbf{Top}</math> sending the object <math>[n]</math> of <math>\Delta</math> to the standard <math>n</math>-simplex inside <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math>.  Finally there is a functor <math>\mathbf{Top} \times \mathbf{Top} \to \mathbf{Top}</math> that takes the product of two topological spaces.


Define <math>S</math> to be the composition of this product functor with <math>dT \times \gamma</math>.  The ''coend'' of <math>S</math> is the geometric realization of <math>T</math>.
